mcqs.question: What should notification infrastructure be provisioned around, given that most events target one user but some target the entire platform?
options: The average event's fan-out, since extreme broadcast events are rare and can be handled with brief queuing delays
The fan-out multiplier of the worst single event you expect, since one broadcast can produce hundreds of millions of sends that must interleave fairly with ordinary traffic
Only push notification volume, since email and SMS have no meaningful capacity limits
Whatever volume the busiest single day of the year happens to produce, ignoring per-event fan-out entirely
mcqs.explanation: A single broadcast event can multiply into hundreds of millions of sends, dwarfing the average per-user event — provisioning for the average would leave the system unable to absorb that spike without starving ordinary traffic. Email and SMS providers do have real rate limits, and per-event fan-out matters independent of overall daily volume.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between deduplication and throttling in a notification pipeline?
options: There is no difference — they solve the same problem and either one alone is sufficient
Deduplication prevents resending the same triggering event twice; throttling caps how many distinct, legitimate notifications one user receives in a short window
Throttling only applies to SMS, and deduplication only applies to push notifications
Deduplication is handled by the channel provider, so the notification system never needs to implement it
mcqs.explanation: Deduplication stops the same event from being sent twice due to at-least-once redelivery; throttling limits the volume of genuinely new, distinct notifications reaching one user in a burst. Both are needed for different reasons, neither is channel-specific, and dedup must be implemented by the notification system itself since providers have no concept of your event IDs.

mcqs.question: A worker pool is dispatching notifications faster than a third-party SMS gateway accepts them, causing throttling errors that are then immediately retried. What's the most direct fix?
options: Retry immediately and more aggressively so the backlog clears faster
Switch entirely to push notifications and drop SMS support
Ignore the throttling errors since they don't affect delivery reliability
Rate-limit sends to that provider on your own side to match its documented ceiling, with backoff, and isolate its queue from other channels
mcqs.explanation: Aggressive immediate retries worsen provider-side throttling rather than clearing it. The correct fix is self-imposed rate limiting matched to the provider's ceiling plus backoff, with each channel's queue isolated so a struggling SMS gateway doesn't stall push or email. Dropping SMS entirely isn't necessary, and throttling errors do mean notifications aren't being delivered.

mcqs.question: A team decides to skip a dedup check before sending because their event queue "rarely" redelivers. What's the flaw in that reasoning?
options: At-least-once delivery is a documented guarantee, not a rare edge case, so redelivery will happen in normal operation and every redelivery becomes a user-visible duplicate without a dedup check
There is no flaw — skipping the dedup check is a reasonable optimization if redelivery is genuinely infrequent
Dedup checks are only necessary for broadcast events, not per-user ones
The event queue provider is responsible for deduplication, not the notification system
mcqs.explanation: At-least-once delivery explicitly allows redelivery as normal, expected behavior, not a rare fault — treating it as unlikely means every redelivery becomes a real duplicate notification a user sees. Dedup matters for events of any size, and most queue providers make no dedup guarantee — that responsibility falls on the consumer.
